connections.feedback: Yes. Changing your mind when you see better information is a strength, not a loss. Checking the message and telling the group helps everyone arrive at the right time.
Saying it first does not make it right. The teacher's message is newer information from the person who decides.
If you say nothing, some people will be early or late. You are the one who gave the first time, so you are the person best placed to fix it.
Going at the right time yourself works for you. But the others still believe 3, so a quick message would have helped them too.
connections.notes: Fixes your own problem; leaves the others uninformed.

Presenting both plans is fair and leaves the choice to the team. But after seeing the new data you have a view, and leaving it out hides what you know.

connections.feedback: Defending a plan because it was yours puts your record ahead of the result. The data is new and deserves a hearing.

connections.feedback: Yes. A week of silence suggests the first mention did not land. Raising it again with numbers and asking who owns the problem moves it forward, and leads to the next level if nobody does.
Waiting is reasonable if the harm is small and your lead is clearly working on it. But a week has already passed with no change, and each week the problem continues has a cost.
connections.notes: Fair if harm is small; the cost grows each week.

connections.feedback: A hidden workaround may fix your part, but it leaves the real cause and the problem for others. It can also confuse people later.
A public complaint puts your lead on the spot before you have used the direct route again. It rarely solves the problem faster.

Another attempt shows persistence and may work. But you have tried twice and the cause is elsewhere, so the cost is more lost time before the people who can help are told.

connections.feedback: Hiding a delay until you have a fix leaves others to plan around a false schedule.
Blaming in a status report puts a second problem on top of the first. State the facts and what you need.

connections.feedback: Yes. The evidence is credible but incomplete, so a fast check of the key figure comes first. Telling stakeholders you are reconsidering is honest and prevents surprises before the renewal date.
Renewing avoids a gap in service. But once signed, a problem found later is harder to act on, so the cost of not checking could be larger.
connections.notes: Avoids disruption; harder to undo if the evidence holds.

connections.feedback: Evidence that is not fully verified is a reason to check, not to reverse yourself at once. Acting before checking swings from one extreme to another.
Having backed the vendor in public does not make them right. Defending out of pride is the problem you were warned about.

connections.feedback: Yes. "Nine out of ten" depends on who was asked. Ten kids picked by the seller is very different from a large, fair group. The question is simple and tells you a lot.
Trying it is the best test of whether you like it. It does not tell you whether the advert's claim is true, which is the question here.
connections.notes: Good for your taste; does not test the claim.

connections.feedback: Adverts often show their best side. The claim may be true, but you cannot tell without knowing who was asked.
Some advert claims are true. Rejecting all of them stops you from learning anything, good or bad.

Reviews from people with no link to the seller are a good check. They are also a small, self-selected sample, so they help but do not settle the question.

connections.feedback: Adverts are made to persuade. A number without a source is a prompt to ask, not a reason to believe.

connections.feedback: Yes. AI summaries can leave out key points, change emphasis or state things the article did not say. Citing a source means you vouch for it, so read the article first.
Stating that an AI wrote it is honest about where the text came from. It still gives your reader an unchecked summary, and many courses do not accept it as a source.
connections.notes: Honest about origin; the content remains unchecked.

connections.feedback: Quick and plausible is not the same as accurate. If the summary is wrong, your paper carries the error under your name.
Using a summary to decide what to read is fine. The mistake is citing it without checking, not using the tool.

connections.feedback: Yes. Confident tone and neat layout are not evidence. AI tools can produce numbers that look real but are not. Find the original source for each figure you plan to use.
Asking the tool to double-check can sometimes catch an obvious slip. But it is the same tool with the same blind spots, so it is not independent verification.
connections.notes: May catch slips; not independent of the original error.

connections.feedback: Your own sense of what is plausible is worth something. But it also tends to confirm what you expect, so a wrong number that fits your expectations is the one you will miss.
connections.notes: Uses your expertise; confirms what you already expect.

connections.feedback: A neat table feels trustworthy because of its look. The look says nothing about where the numbers came from.

connections.feedback: Yes. A story can show a real problem exists and is a good reason to look. How common it is decides whether a major change is justified, and that needs data.
The harm described sounds real and deserves action. But a policy change affects everyone, so the story alone does not show whether the problem is common enough to justify it.
connections.notes: Takes harm seriously; skips the question of how common it is.

connections.feedback: One story is not proof of a pattern, but it can point to one. Dismissing it throws away a useful lead.
Stories are vivid, which is why they persuade. Vividness is not the same as being typical.

connections.feedback: Yes. A demo shows the best case. A short trial on low-risk replies, reviewed by a person, shows how the tool fails in your own work and keeps the cost of mistakes low.
Reviewing every reply is a good safeguard. But the tool is untested on your work, and reviewers tend to approve what looks fluent, so errors may pass through at scale.
connections.notes: Has a safeguard; scales before the failure pattern is known.

connections.feedback: A ban removes the risk while you learn. It also gives up possible benefits and may push people to use the tool unofficially, without any rules.
connections.notes: Cautious; may drive use out of sight.

connections.feedback: A good demo is made to impress. It does not show what happens with unusual or sensitive requests.
